$comment: The quality contract for the agent, as a reviewable file.
'floor' is an absolute minimum the scorer must clear on every run.
'maxRegression' is how far a scorer may fall against the base experiment,
as an absolute drop in the 0-1 score.
Measured baseline (v1-grounded, claude-haiku-4-5, 35 cases x 3 trials):
answer_quality 55.0%  citation_grounding 100%  tool_selection 100%
trajectory_efficiency 93.8%  count_accuracy 100%
Two scorers deliberately have NO floor, for the same reason:
answer_quality is an LLM judge. autoevals' Factuality scores a correct
answer that says MORE than the reference as a 'superset' worth 0.6, and
the reference answers here are terse. So its absolute level mostly
encodes rubric and reference style, not agent quality — 55% is a
verbose-but-correct agent, not a failing one. The number is meaningful
as a delta between runs that share a rubric, so it is gated on
regression only. The first floor here was 0.6, guessed before any run;
measuring showed it was testing the fixture rather than the agent.
trajectory_efficiency rewards fewer tool calls. A floor would push
toward exactly the behaviour citation_grounding and tool_selection
exist to prevent.
The deterministic scorers keep tight floors, because for those an
absolute number does mean something: an ID nobody looked up is wrong at
any threshold.
